transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I guess I'm here because things have just gotten so out of hand where I live. I mean, it's not just a feeling, I know for an absolute fact that the people at my apartment complex are watching me. Every single time I leave my door, every time I come back from the store or even just take the trash out, there's always someone peering out their window or standing in the hallway, just... monitoring my comings and goings. And it doesn't stop there, either. They're actually slipping notes about me to the leasing office. I've seen the papers. Now, the manager and my sister and everybody else, they keep telling me, "Oh, it's just regular notices, they're just putting flyers on everyone's doors," but I know better. You can tell by the way they look at me when they do it, and the timing of it all. It's just too coordinated, you know? It's exhausting having to be on guard all the time, constantly wondering what they're writing about me and why they're so fixated on my schedule.
Have you been feeling unusually energized, irritable, or down in the dumps for a significant period of time recently?

Energized? No, no, definitely not energized. If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. I haven't had real energy in... well, I don't even know how long. But as for feeling down, yes. Very much so. 

It's... well, for a long while now, I just feel so incredibly low. Like, most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling right in the middle of my chest. It's like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor, you know? I'll just open my eyes and lie there, staring up at the ceiling—there's this little water stain right near the bedroom fan that I just look at for God knows how long—and I just feel so totally empty. 

I don't have a job to rush off to or a time clock to punch anymore, so I just sit there on the edge of the mattress, rubbing my face, trying to find a single good reason to stand up. It's like I'm wearing a lead vest or trying to walk through wet cement. My sister, she calls and says, "You need to get up, make some breakfast, open the blinds," but she doesn't understand how hard it is when you're carrying around that kind of heaviness from the second you wake up. It's not just being a little sad, it's like someone scooped out my insides and left this big, heavy void. So yeah, "down in the dumps" is putting it mildly, Dr. Smith. It's every single morning, just this dragging, miserable weight before the day even really starts.
Have you experienced these thoughts about people watching you or leaving you notes even during times when you weren't feeling this deep sense of sadness?

Well, let me think about that. You know, it's funny you bring that up, because... well, yes. Yes, I have. See, there was this spell not too long ago—maybe a month or two back, I lose track of the exact days since I don't punch a clock anymore—but there was a stretch of several weeks where I was actually doing a bit better. The heavy feeling kind of lifted for a bit. I was actually eating better, going down to the grocery store and buying cold cuts, the honey ham I like, making real sandwiches instead of just sitting there staring at the wall. 

And I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless every single morning. My sister even called me up and said I sounded a lot more like my old self on the phone, which was nice to hear, you know? I wasn't dreading the sun coming up. But the thing is, Dr. Smith, even when I was feeling decent, even when I didn't have that awful weight on my chest, I still knew exactly what was going on outside my door. I still knew for an absolute fact that the neighbors were watching me. 

I'd go out to check the mail or take my little bag of trash to the chute, feeling perfectly fine, not sad at all, and I'd still catch them peeking through their blinds. I knew they were still reporting on me to the leasing office. It didn't matter one bit that I wasn't feeling down in the dumps, they were still keeping their logs and slipping those notes about me to the manager. It just never stops with them, no matter how I'm feeling inside. So yeah, the sadness took a break for a few weeks, it really did, but the spying? That just kept right on going. Every single time I opened my door, there they were, just waiting to see what I was doing so they could write it down...
Aside from the belief that your neighbors are watching you, have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear?

Voices? Like... like people talking when nobody's in the room? No. No, definitely not. I'm not hearing things that aren't there, if that's what you're getting at. I know the difference between what's real and what's not. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, I hear plenty of noises, but that's just because that building is so old and cheap. The walls are basically made of tissue paper. I can hear the pipes clanking in the walls all winter, and I can hear the floorboards groaning when the guy upstairs—I think he works construction or something—when he walks around in his heavy boots at all hours. And I definitely hear the neighbors out in the hall when they're creeping around my door. I can hear the rubber on their shoes squeaking on the linoleum, and I hear them whispering to each other when they're getting ready to slide one of those notes to the manager. 

My sister, she actually asked me the same kind of thing once. She said, "Are you sure you're not just imagining the sounds? Maybe it's just the wind or the building settling." And I had to tell her, look, I'm fifty-nine years old, I've been around long enough to know what real people sound like. When I hear them outside my door, it's because they are physically out there, standing on the mat, trying to be quiet but failing at it. But as for, you know, voices inside my head, or people talking to me from the empty corners of the ceiling or something? No, nothing like that at all. I don't have that problem. My problem is the actual, flesh-and-blood people living next to me who won't mind their own business and keep tracking my every move. So no, no imaginary voices. Just the real ones out in the hallway that shouldn't be there in the first place.

Have you noticed that, over these past few months, you've lost interest in hobbies or activities you used to enjoy, or that you've been having more trouble than usual keeping up with basic things like personal hygiene or cleaning your home?

Well, yeah. I mean, it's funny you mention the hobbies and the cleaning, because... well, it's all tied up in that heavy feeling I was telling you about. You know, before all this, before I felt like I was wearing that lead vest every day, I used to do a lot. I really did. I wasn't just sitting around staring at a water stain, that's for sure. 

Take Sundays, for example. Sundays used to be my big day. I'd get up early, put on a pot of coffee, and I'd start a big pot of beans on the stove. I had this whole recipe, you know, with the ham hocks and the onions, let it simmer all day long. The whole apartment would smell like it. And then I'd head over to the church for choir practice. I've got—well, I used to have—a pretty decent baritone. We'd practice for two hours, and I actually looked forward to it. It felt good to sing, to be around the other folks. And on Thursdays, I'd go down to the community center and play bridge. I'm pretty sharp at cards, or at least I was. Plus, I was always good with my hands, so I'd do these little repair jobs for folks in the building. You know, fixing a leaky faucet, swapping out a bad light switch, hanging a heavy mirror. Kept me busy. Kept me feeling useful, I guess.

But now? Now... I don't know. It's like a switch just got flipped off inside me. I don't even buy beans anymore, let alone cook them. The thought of standing over a stove for hours just seems... impossible. And the choir? The bridge games? I haven't been in months. The phone will ring—it'll be Mrs. Higgins from down the hall asking if I can look at her radiator, or maybe one of the guys from the bridge club—and I just sit there on the edge of the bed and listen to it ring. I'll just stare at it and tell myself, "There's no point. What's the point of going? What's the point of doing any of it?" 

It's just too much effort. Everything is too much effort. Even taking a shower, you mentioned hygiene... some days, the thought of turning on the water and standing there, it's just exhausting before I even do it. So I just let the phone ring, and I let the dust gather, and I just stay right where I am. Because honestly, Dr. Smith, I just can't find a single reason to care about any of those things anymore.
Looking back over the last year or two, were there any periods where you felt this deep, heavy sadness for weeks at a time, but during those specific weeks, the neighbors were not spying on you?

Well, now... no. No, it definitely doesn't work like that. It's not like they take a vacation just because I'm having a hard time. If I'm really looking back over the last year or two, like you're asking, it's actually... well, it's almost the exact opposite. 

See, when I get really low, when I'm just sinking down into that... that deep, hollow place, you know? The times when I'm barely eating anything, maybe just staring at a cold can of soup on the counter, and I'm definitely not answering the phone when it rings... during those specific weeks, that is actually when I am the most sure that the apartment people are tracking me. 

I mean, I'll be sitting there in the dark, feeling like I can't even lift my arms because of the weight of it all, but I still know exactly what's happening outside my door. I am absolutely certain they are out there taking their little notes and talking to the office about me. It's like... it's like they know I'm vulnerable, maybe? I don't know why they do it, but I just know that when I'm at my absolute worst, when that sadness is just swallowing me whole, that's when I'm the most convinced they're keeping tabs on me and reporting back to the manager. 

So no, the spying doesn't stop when the sadness gets heavy. I'll just be sitting there, completely hollowed out, not doing a single thing, and I'll know for a fact they're out in the hall tracking my every non-move. It never takes a break, Dr. Smith, not even when I'm at rock bottom.
